title: Ships 'with upright horns' (orthokrairai)
greek: νεῶν ὀρθοκραιράων (neōn orthokrairaōn)
short: An epithet transferred from cattle to ships: the high curving stem and stern of early ships looked like the horns of an ox.
body: The adjective orthokrairos, 'with upright horns', is used literally of cattle (8.231; on the Shield, 18.573) and metaphorically of ships here and at 19.344. Leaf quotes the ancient scholion, which explains it as a metaphor from oxen because the prows and sterns of ships rose up high, and he relates it to the oldest Greek ships, which before the beaked prow ended in vertical ornaments (aphlasta) at stem and stern, naturally suggesting horns. Leaf's Companion says the same of the upright 'ensigns' at either end of the ship (cf. 9.241). The phrase sets Akhilleus 'before the ships' at the opening of the book, apart from the fighting and already anxious, as he sees the Achaeans driven back across the plain and remembers a prophecy of his mother.

title: Akhilleus' mourning for Patroclus
greek: αὐτὸς δ᾽ ἐν κονίῃσι μέγας μεγαλωστὶ τανυσθεὶς κεῖτο (autos d' en koniēisi megas megalōsti tanustheis keito)
short: Akhilleus pours ash over his head, lies outstretched in the dust and tears his hair, gestures of a mourner that also make him look like a corpse.
body: Akhilleus performs the traditional acts of lamentation: he pours dark dust on his head, defiles his face, lies stretched in the dust 'mighty in his mightiness' (megas megalōsti) and tears his hair; the captive women beat their breasts. The phrase megas megalōsti is used of the dead Cebriones (16.776) and, in the Odyssey, of Akhilleus' own corpse (Od. 24.39-40): the mourner already looks like the dead man he will become. Antilochus holds his hands for fear he will cut his throat 'with the iron'; Leaf's Companion suggests a knife rather than a sword, since Homeric weapons are bronze but small tools often iron. Plato objected to such scenes: the Republic (388a-b) asks poets not to show the son of a goddess strewing ash over his head and lamenting. Kakridis and later neoanalysts argued that this scene, with Thetis and the Nereids, echoes an older poem on Akhilleus' death and funeral.

title: The catalogue of Nereids
greek: Γλαύκη τε Θάλειά τε Κυμοδόκη τε (Glaukē te Thaleia te Kumodokē te)
short: Thetis' sisters, daughters of the sea-god Nereus, gather to lament; their names describe the sea. Ancient critics thought the list un-Homeric.
body: Hearing Akhilleus groan, Thetis cries out in the depths 'beside the old man her father', Nereus, and her sisters gather round her. Their names are 'speaking names' drawn from the sea: Glauce ('grey-blue'), Cymodoce ('wave-receiver'), Thoe ('swift'), Speio ('of the cave'), Nemertes ('unerring') and Apseudes ('truthful', recalling Nereus' own truthfulness), Galatea ('milk-white'). The scholia report that Zenodotus marked lines 39-49 as spurious because the catalogue had a 'Hesiodic character': Homer, they argued, speaks of Muses or Eileithyiai collectively, without naming them. Leaf agreed, observing that the names seem selected from Hesiod's longer list of fifty Nereids (Theogony 240-64), where Nereus is called 'the Old Man' because he is truthful and gentle. Modern commentators such as Edwards are more willing to keep the list as a deliberate ornament: the sisters form a chorus for Thetis' lament, as they will at Akhilleus' real funeral (Od. 24.47-59).

title: Thetis' lament: dusaristotokeia
greek: ὤ μοι δυσαριστοτόκεια (ō moi dusaristotokeia)
short: Thetis calls herself 'unhappy mother of the best of men', one compound word, and mourns her living son as if he were already dead.
body: The Greek coins a single word for Thetis' grief, dusaristotokeia, 'unhappy mother of the noblest son' (LSJ); the scholion quoted by Leaf glosses it as 'having borne the best to misfortune'. Her speech has the form of a funeral lament (goos), though Akhilleus is alive: she raised him like a young plant in an orchard (ernei isos, 'like a sapling', a metaphor Leaf traces in Od. 6.162 and 14.175), sent him to Troy, and will never welcome him home. When she reaches him she cries out and takes his head in her hands (18.71), the gesture of the chief mourner over a corpse (Akhilleus over Patroclus, 23.136; Andromache over Hector, 24.724). Plato quotes this very line among the passages he would ban, since gods should not be shown lamenting (Republic 388c). Many scholars since Kakridis read the scene as an anticipation of Thetis' lament at Akhilleus' own funeral (Od. 24.47-62).

title: The plan of Zeus fulfilled
greek: τὰ μὲν δή τοι τετέλεσται ἐκ Διός (ta men dē toi tetelestai ek Dios)
short: Thetis reminds Akhilleus that his prayer from Book 1 has been granted; he answers that it brings no pleasure, since Patroclus is dead.
body: Thetis recalls the prayer of Book 1: Akhilleus asked that the Achaeans be pinned against their ships and suffer, so that they would learn his worth (1.407-12), and Zeus nodded his assent (1.524-30). That is the 'plan of Zeus' announced in the poem's fifth line, and it has now been 'accomplished'. Akhilleus' answer is one of the turning-points of the poem: 'what pleasure have I therein', since he has lost Patroclus, 'whom I honoured above all my comrades, even as mine own self' (literally 'equal to my own head', ison emēi kephalēi). The granting of the wish has destroyed what he valued most. Laura Slatkin has shown how Thetis' power over Zeus, rooted in older myth, and her helplessness to save her own son shape the Iliad's treatment of Akhilleus' mortality.

sources.cite: Laura M. Slatkin, The Power of Thetis: Allusion and Interpretation in the Iliad (Berkeley, 1991; rev. ed. Center for Hellenic Studies, 2011), ch. 1, 'The Helplessness of Thetis'

anchor: the bed of a mortal man
title: The wedding of Peleus and Thetis
greek: ἤματι τῷ ὅτε σε βροτοῦ ἀνέρος ἔμβαλον εὐνῇ (ēmati tōi hote se brotou aneros embalon eunēi)
short: The armour Hector took was the gods' gift to Peleus when they married Thetis to a mortal; Akhilleus wishes the marriage had never happened.
body: The gods attended the wedding of Peleus and the sea-goddess Thetis and gave splendid gifts: the armour (here and 17.195-6), the immortal horses (16.381, 17.443-4), and, in later accounts, the ash spear from Chiron (Apollodorus 3.13.5). The marriage was not a happy one for Thetis: she tells Hephaestus that Zeus 'subdued' her alone of the sea-goddesses to a mortal, and that she endured his bed 'sore against my will' (18.432-4). Later poets explain why: Zeus and Poseidon gave her up because it was foretold that her son would be greater than his father (Pindar, Isthmian 8.26-47). The Cypria made the wedding the place where Strife began the quarrel that led to the Trojan War. Akhilleus' wish that Peleus had married a mortal bride is thus a wish that he himself had never been born, so that his mother would not have to grieve.

sources.cite: Apollodorus, Library 3.13.5 (trans. J. G. Frazer)

anchor: Doomed then to a speedy death
title: Akhilleus' choice: ōkumoros, 'swift-doomed'
greek: ὠκύμορος δή μοι τέκος ἔσσεαι ... αὐτίκα γάρ τοι ἔπειτα μεθ᾽ Ἕκτορα πότμος ἑτοῖμος (ōkumoros dē moi tekos esseai ... autika gar toi epeita meth' Hektora potmos hetoimos)
short: Thetis warns that Akhilleus' death will follow Hector's at once; he accepts, choosing glory and revenge over life.
body: Ōkumoros, 'swift-fated, dying early', is Thetis' word for Akhilleus from the start (1.417, 1.505) and LSJ lists these passages. In Book 9 Akhilleus told the envoys of his two fates: a short life with undying glory at Troy or a long life without it at home (9.410-16). Now the choice becomes concrete: if he kills Hector, his own death is 'ready at hand'. His reply, 'Straightway may I die', since he failed to help his comrade, settles the matter. He calls himself a useless burden on the earth (etōsion achthos arourēs, compared by Leaf with Od. 20.379), and resolves to win 'glorious renown' (kleos esthlon) and accept death 'whenso Zeus willeth'. From here onward Akhilleus fights as a man who knows he is about to die.

title: 'May strife perish': Akhilleus renounces his anger
greek: ὡς ἔρις ἔκ τε θεῶν ἔκ τ᾽ ἀνθρώπων ἀπόλοιτο καὶ χόλος (hōs eris ek te theōn ek t' anthrōpōn apoloito kai cholos)
short: Akhilleus curses strife and anger, 'sweeter than dripping honey', which swells like smoke; Heraclitus famously objected that without strife the world would perish.
body: Akhilleus wishes that strife (eris) would vanish from gods and men, and with it anger (cholos), which 'setteth a man on to grow wroth, how wise soever he be' and is 'sweeter far than trickling honey', growing in the breast like smoke. Leaf's Companion compares the honey to Jonathan tasting the dripping honey in the wood (1 Samuel 14:25-7) and explains the smoke: a little fire soon fills a whole house. The line became famous in philosophy. Aristotle reports that Heraclitus rebuked the poet who wrote 'would strife might perish from gods and men', since there would be no harmony without high and low notes, nor animals without male and female (Eudemian Ethics 7.1, 1235a25-9; Leaf cites the passage). The renunciation is real but limited: Akhilleus lays aside his wrath against Agamemnon only to redirect a fiercer anger against Hector.

sources.cite: Aristotle, Eudemian Ethics 7.1, 1235a25-9 (trans. H. Rackham)

title: The example of Heracles
greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ βίη Ἡρακλῆος φύγε κῆρα (oude gar oude biē Hēraklēos phuge kēra)
short: Not even Heracles, dearest to Zeus, escaped death: Akhilleus uses the greatest hero as a paradigm for accepting his own fate.
body: Akhilleus consoles himself with a mythological example (paradeigma), a common Homeric form of persuasion: 'not even the mighty Heracles escaped death', though he was dearest to Zeus, for fate (moira) and 'the dread wrath of Hera' overcame him. Hera's persecution of Heracles is told elsewhere in the Iliad (14.249-56, 15.18-30, and the story of her trick at his birth, 19.95-133). Leaf points out that this passage knows nothing of Heracles' later apotheosis, his elevation to Olympus, which first appears in Od. 11.602-4, lines suspected in antiquity. For Akhilleus, then, Heracles' fame survives but Heracles himself is dead; Akhilleus chooses the same bargain, death followed by kleos esthlon, 'good fame'. The parallel also sets up an irony: both heroes suffer through a goddess's anger and the will of Zeus.

title: Akhilleus at the trench
greek: ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ κεφαλῇ νέφος ἔστεφε δῖα θεάων χρύσεον, ἐκ δ᾽ αὐτοῦ δαῖε φλόγα παμφανόωσαν (amphi de hoi kephalēi nephos estephe dia theaōn chruseon, ek d' autou daie phloga pamphanoōsan)
short: Unarmed, Akhilleus appears at the trench wrapped in Athena's aegis and a golden cloud, with fire blazing from his head; his three shouts rout the Trojans.
body: Iris, sent by Hera without Zeus' knowledge, tells Akhilleus to show himself at the trench even without armour. Athena throws the aegis round his shoulders and sets a golden cloud on his head, from which a flame blazes; he shouts three times, Athena's voice joins his, and twelve Trojans die in the confusion among their own chariots. Fire about the head marks a hero at the height of his power (Diomedes in 5.4-7; Akhilleus again in 19.374-83 and 22.134-5). Leaf's Companion calls the appearance at the trench 'one of the supreme pieces of poetical imagination which the world has brought forth', though as an analyst he dated the trench scene late. Akhilleus wins the body back by voice and presence alone, before Hephaestus has made his new arms. Tennyson translated the passage as 'Achilles over the Trench' (1877).

title: The beacon-fire simile
greek: πυρσοί τε φλεγέθουσιν ἐπήτριμοι (pursoi te phlegethousin epētrimoi)
short: The light from Akhilleus' head is like smoke and then signal-fires rising at sunset from a besieged island town calling for help.
body: An island town is under attack; all day its men fight from the walls, and at sunset they light beacon after beacon so that neighbours may come in ships to help. Leaf explains the point: beacons show only smoke by day and only fire by night, but at sunset both are seen together, just as fire shines through the dark cloud over Akhilleus' head. The mixture of light and darkness conveys a lurid gloom, as in the rainbow simile of 17.547. The simile is rich in irony: it pictures a besieged city praying for rescue, exactly Troy's situation, yet the 'warder off of bane' it evokes is Akhilleus, Troy's destroyer, coming to save the Achaeans. It prepares the besieged city on the Shield.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Macmillan, 1902), note on 18.207

title: The trumpet (salpinx)
greek: ὅτε τ᾽ ἴαχε σάλπιγξ (hote t' iache salpinx)
short: Akhilleus' voice rings like a war-trumpet: the only trumpet in Homer appears in a simile, never in the heroes' own battles.
body: LSJ cites this line as the earliest instance of salpinx, 'war-trumpet'. Homeric heroes never use trumpets: armies are roused by heralds and by the shouts of men like Stentor 'with voice of bronze' (5.785-6). The ancient commentators noticed this and remarked, as Leaf quotes, that the poet himself knows trumpets but does not bring the heroes using them; the only other reference is a metaphor, when 'great heaven trumpeted round about' as the gods join battle (21.388). Leaf's Companion concludes that the poet knew the trumpet as a recent invention and kept it out of the heroic world, using it only in comparisons drawn from his audience's experience. The 'brazen voice' of Akhilleus (18.222) continues the image. The passage is a good example of how similes open a window on the poet's own time.

title: Hera sends the sun down: the end of the great day of battle
greek: Ἠέλιον δ᾽ ἀκάμαντα βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη πέμψεν ἐπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοὰς ἀέκοντα νέεσθαι (Ēelion d' akamanta boōpis potnia Hērē pempsen ep' Ōkeanoio rhoas aekonta neesthai)
short: Hera forces the reluctant sun to set early, ending the single long day of fighting that began at dawn in Book 11.
body: The battle that began at dawn in Book 11 (11.1-2) has run without a break through Books 11-18, covering the wounding of the Achaean leaders, the fight at the wall and ships, Patroclus' aristeia and death, and the struggle for his body. Zeus had promised Hector victory 'until the sun sets and sacred darkness comes on' (11.191-4, 17.453-5). Hera, eager to end Hector's day of glory, now makes the 'unwearying' sun go down to the stream of Ocean against his will. Leaf's Companion observes that this is the only case in Homer where a god interferes with the course of nature in this way, apart from Athena holding back the dawn in Od. 23.241-6; as an analyst he also noted that the quantity of events crowded into this one day fits awkwardly with an early sunset. The early night gives the Trojans their fateful assembly.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, A Companion to the Iliad for English Readers (Macmillan, 1892), p. 301-302, note on 18.239

anchor: looked at once before and after
title: Polydamas, the man who 'looked before and after'
greek: ὃ γὰρ οἶος ὅρα πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω ... ἰῇ δ᾽ ἐν νυκτὶ γένοντο (ho gar oios hora prossō kai opissō ... iēi d' en nukti genonto)
short: Hector's prudent twin in counsel, born the same night, advises retreat into the city; Hector rejects him, a choice he will regret before his death.
body: Polydamas, son of Panthous (and brother of Euphorbus), was born on the same night as Hector: 'one excelled in speech, the other with the spear'. The poem pairs them as complementary halves of Trojan leadership, and Polydamas advises Hector four times (12.60-80, 12.210-50, 13.725-53, and here). He 'alone looked before and after'; Leaf argues that the phrase is spatial rather than temporal, describing a man who takes a wide view instead of fixing his eyes on what is just in front of him (compare 1.343, 3.109). His advice now is sound: Akhilleus is back, so the Trojans should withdraw behind their walls before dawn. Hector angrily rejects it, and the Trojans applaud, 'fools that they were' (18.310-13). When Hector waits alone for Akhilleus outside the walls, he remembers that Polydamas will be the first to reproach him (22.99-103): his shame (aidōs) at this rejected counsel keeps him outside to die.

title: 'The war-god is impartial' (xunos Enualios)
greek: ξυνὸς Ἐνυάλιος, καί τε κτανέοντα κατέκτα (xunos Enualios, kai te ktaneonta katekta)
short: Hector answers with a proverb: the war-god is common to both sides and kills the would-be killer. The narrator calls the applauding Trojans fools.
body: Hector closes his reply to Polydamas with a maxim: 'common to all is Enyalius (Ares), and he slays the one who would slay'. Leaf compares 'victory shifts from man to man' (6.339). The saying was already proverbial in antiquity: Aristotle's Rhetoric (2.21.11, 1395a) recommends using well-worn maxims because their very commonness makes them seem true, and cites this one as the encouragement suited to soldiers outnumbered by the enemy. The proverb is true, and it will apply to Hector himself, who killed Patroclus and will be killed by Akhilleus. The narrator immediately comments that the Trojans who cheered were 'fools' (nēpioi), since Pallas Athena had taken away their wits: they praised Hector's bad counsel and nobody praised Polydamas, who had advised well. Hector's confidence comes from his day of success, granted by Zeus only until sunset.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Macmillan, 1902), note on 18.309
Aristotle, Rhetoric 2.21.11, 1395a (trans. J. H. Freese)

title: Akhilleus as a lion robbed of its cubs
greek: ὥς τε λὶς ἠϋγένειος, ᾧ ῥά θ᾽ ὑπὸ σκύμνους ἐλαφηβόλος ἁρπάσῃ ἀνήρ (hōs te lis ēugeneios, hōi rha th' hupo skumnous elaphēbolos harpasēi anēr)
short: Laying his 'man-slaying hands' on Patroclus' breast, Akhilleus groans like a lion whose cubs a hunter has stolen, and who tracks the man in rage.
body: Akhilleus leads the lament, placing his 'man-slaying hands' on his friend's breast. The poet sets the murderous hands beside their tender use, a contrast developed further when Priam kisses 'the terrible, man-slaying hands' that killed his sons (24.478-9). The simile of the lion whose cubs a stag-hunter has carried off answers Ajax's lion guarding its cubs in 17.133-6: protection has failed, and grief turns to a hunt for the killer, 'for anger exceeding grim layeth hold of him'. Ancient critics worried about the zoology, since it is the lioness that rears cubs (compare the objection Leaf records on 17.134-6); Homer's word lis/leōn can cover either sex. The simile thus pictures Akhilleus as a bereaved parent, and turns his grief directly into the pursuit of Hector.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Macmillan, 1902), note on 18.318

title: Opoeis (Opous), Patroclus' home
greek: εἰς Ὀπόεντα (eis Opoenta)
short: Opous in eastern Locris, from which Patroclus came; Akhilleus had promised his father Menoetius to bring him home with spoils.
body: Opoeis, later Opous, was the chief town of the Opuntian (eastern) Locrians in central Greece, on the coast opposite Euboea. Patroclus' ghost tells the story of his exile in 23.84-90: as a boy he killed a playmate in anger over a game of knucklebones, and his father Menoetius brought him from Opous to Peleus in Phthia, where he was raised with Akhilleus. Leaf's Companion notes that Patroclus left his home there after a homicide. In 18.324-6 Akhilleus recalls that he had promised Menoetius to bring his son home with his share of the spoil. The promise frames the theme of nostos (homecoming) denied: Akhilleus now knows that both of them 'are fated to redden the selfsame earth' at Troy. Pindar's ninth Olympian, for an athlete of Opous, also celebrates Menoetius and Patroclus as heroes of the city.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, A Companion to the Iliad for English Readers (Macmillan, 1892), p. 303, note on 18.326

anchor: twelve glorious sons of the Trojans
title: The vow of human sacrifice
greek: δώδεκα δὲ προπάροιθε πυρῆς ἀποδειροτομήσω Τρώων ἀγλαὰ τέκνα (dōdeka de proparoithe purēs apodeirotomēsō Trōōn aglaa tekna)
short: Akhilleus vows not to bury Patroclus until he brings Hector's head and armour, and to cut the throats of twelve Trojan youths at the pyre.
body: Akhilleus' vow sets the programme for the rest of the poem: Patroclus will lie unburied until Hector's armour and head are brought, and twelve noble Trojan youths will be slaughtered before the pyre in revenge. He captures them alive in the river (21.26-32), where they are called a poinē, a 'price' or 'penalty', for Patroclus (LSJ cites the line), and kills them at the funeral (23.175-6), where the narrator comments that 'he devised evil deeds in his heart'. Leaf notes that 18.336-7 recur in 23.22-3 and suggests either that the promise was simply repeated or that the lines were inserted here to prepare the episode of Book 23. Human sacrifice is otherwise almost absent from Homer; its appearance here measures how far grief and anger have carried Akhilleus beyond the norms of war.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Macmillan, 1902), note on 18.336

title: Preparing the body for burial
greek: ἐν δ᾽ ὠτειλὰς πλῆσαν ἀλείφατος ἐννεώροιο (en d' ōteilas plēsan aleiphatos enneōroio)
short: Patroclus' body is washed with warm water, anointed, his wounds filled with nine-year-old unguent, and laid on a bier under linen and a white cloak.
body: The scene shows the first stage of a Homeric funeral: water heated in a cauldron, the body washed and anointed with oil, the wounds filled with ointment, then laid on a bed and covered with a fine linen sheet from head to foot and a white cloak (pharos), followed by lament through the night. The same sequence is used for Akhilleus' own body (Od. 24.43-6) and for Hector's when Priam ransoms it (24.580-90). Leaf explains enneōros, 'nine years old', as indicating full maturity: oil apparently improved with keeping, and 'nine' was a traditional round number, as in Minos ruling 'nine years' (Od. 19.179). Patroclus will lie in this state, mourned by the captive women, until Akhilleus has fulfilled his vow; the full funeral and games come only in Book 23.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Macmillan, 1902), note on 18.351

title: Hephaestus' house: self-moving tripods and golden maids
greek: ὄφρά οἱ αὐτόματοι θεῖον δυσαίατ᾽ ἀγῶνα (ophra hoi automatoi theion dusaiat' agōna)
short: Hephaestus is making wheeled tripods that move by themselves, and is served by golden maidens with minds and voices: the first automata in Greek literature.
body: Thetis finds the god in his starry bronze house making twenty tripods on golden wheels that go 'of themselves' (automatoi) to the gods' assembly and back. Leaf compares wheeled stands in Phoenician work and the brazen wheels of Solomon's temple bases (1 Kings 7:27-38), and the gold and silver dogs Hephaestus made for Alcinous (Od. 7.91-4); he notes how sparingly Homer uses such marvels even on Olympus. Hephaestus is then helped by maidservants 'wrought of gold' who have understanding, speech and strength (18.417-21). Aristotle (Politics 1.4, 1253b33-1254a1) cites these tripods: if tools could do their work at command, like the tripods of Hephaestus that 'enter self-moved the company divine', masters would not need slaves. Leaf explains the 'starry' house (asteroeis) as decorated with star-like bosses, as perhaps in the tholos tomb called the 'Treasury of Atreus' at Mycenae.

anchor: god of the two strong arms
title: Amphigueeis: 'of the two strong arms' or 'lame in both legs'?
greek: περικλυτὸς ἀμφιγυήεις (periklutos amphiguēeis); κυλλοποδίων (kullopodiōn)
short: Murray translates Hephaestus' epithet as 'of the two strong arms'; many scholars think it means 'crooked in both legs', referring to his lameness.
body: Amphiguēeis is one of Hephaestus' standing epithets, and its meaning was disputed in antiquity. One tradition, followed by Murray, took it as 'strong (or skilled) in both arms, ambidextrous', fitting a smith. Leaf objects that nothing in the word expresses strength, and prefers 'with a crooked limb on each side', equivalent to kullopodiōn, 'club-footed, halting' (LSJ), used of the god at 18.371. That sense agrees with the text: Hephaestus rises 'a huge, panting bulk, halting', his 'slender legs' moving nimbly beneath him, and leans on golden maids (18.410-21). The two readings need not exclude each other: a lame god with powerful arms is exactly the figure Book 18 presents. The epithet marks the paradox of the divine craftsman: crippled and mocked on Olympus (1.599-600), yet the maker of the most wonderful objects in the poem.

title: Hephaestus' fall, Eurynome and Charis
greek: μητρὸς ἐμῆς ἰότητι κυνώπιδος, ἥ μ᾽ ἐθέλησε κρύψαι χωλὸν ἐόντα (mētros emēs iotēti kunōpidos, hē m' ethelēse krupsai chōlon eonta)
short: Hephaestus recalls how his 'dog-faced' mother Hera threw him from heaven for his lameness, and how Thetis and Eurynome saved him.
body: Hephaestus owes Thetis a debt: when Hera, ashamed of his lameness, cast him out of heaven, Thetis and Eurynome, daughter of 'backward-flowing' Ocean, received him, and for nine years he made jewellery in their sea-cave. In Book 1 a different story is told: Zeus threw him down for helping Hera, and he fell on Lemnos (1.590-4). Leaf notes the difference and that Hera and Hephaestus are usually close allies. Hera's epithet kunōpis, 'dog-eyed, shameless', is the insult Akhilleus throws at Agamemnon (1.159) and Helen at herself (3.180). The god's wife here is Charis ('Grace'); in the Odyssey he is married to Aphrodite (Od. 8.266-366). Leaf, following the scholion, calls Charis a transparent allegory, since grace must accompany craft. Fittingly, Hesiod makes Eurynome the mother of the Graces (Theogony 907-9) and names the youngest, Aglaea, as Hephaestus' wife (945-6).

title: Thetis supplicates Hephaestus
greek: τοὔνεκα νῦν τὰ σὰ γούναθ᾽ ἱκάνομαι (touneka nun ta sa gounath' hikanomai)
short: Thetis comes 'to the knees' of Hephaestus as a suppliant, retelling her sorrows; he promises arms that men will marvel at, though they cannot save her son.
body: Supplication (hiketeia) was a ritualised appeal: the suppliant clasped the knees (or chin) of the person addressed and recalled past services, placing the other under religious obligation to grant the request; John Gould's classic study analyses its forms. Thetis has supplicated Zeus in the same way in Book 1 (1.500-12). Here she recounts her life: forced alone among the sea-goddesses to marry a mortal, Peleus, now worn by old age; mother of a son 'doomed to a speedy death'; and a summary of the Iliad's plot from Briseis to Patroclus' death. Aristarchus rejected the recapitulation (444-56) as unnecessary, according to Leaf's Companion. Hephaestus' answer is a masterpiece of tragic irony; Leaf explains its form: 'he shall have his armour as surely as I cannot save him from death'. The marvellous arms will bring glory, not survival.

title: The Shield of Akhilleus
greek: ποίει δὲ πρώτιστα σάκος μέγα τε στιβαρόν τε ... πέντε δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἔσαν σάκεος πτύχες (poiei de prōtista sakos mega te stibaron te ... pente d' ar' autou esan sakeos ptuches)
short: Hephaestus forges a great shield of five layers decorated with the cosmos, two cities, the farming year, a dance and the encircling Ocean: Western literature's founding ekphrasis.
body: Hephaestus puts bronze, tin, gold and silver in the fire and makes a shield with a triple rim and five layers (ptuches), which Leaf takes to be hides behind a metal facing; the scenes are on the surface. Leaf's Companion connects the technique with the inlaid dagger-blades from Mycenae, where coloured metals make pictures on a dark bronze ground, and argues that the scenes are arranged in concentric bands, with heavenly bodies at the centre and the river Ocean at the rim (18.607-8). The description is the model of ekphrasis, the verbal description of a work of art, imitated in the Hesiodic Shield of Heracles and Virgil's Shield of Aeneas (Aeneid 8.626-728), and answered in modern times by W. H. Auden's 'The Shield of Achilles' (1952). Lessing (Laocoön, 1766, ch. 18) admired how Homer describes the shield by narrating its making, so that the scenes move and sound. Oliver Taplin has shown how its world of peace and work frames the war.

title: The constellations on the Shield
greek: Πληϊάδας θ᾽ Ὑάδας τε τό τε σθένος Ὠρίωνος Ἄρκτόν θ᾽ ... οἴη δ᾽ ἄμμορός ἐστι λοετρῶν Ὠκεανοῖο (Plēiadas th' Huadas te to te sthenos Ōriōnos Arkton th' ... oiē d' ammoros esti loetrōn Ōkeanoio)
short: At the shield's centre are earth, sky, sea, sun, moon and the stars, including the Bear that alone never bathes in Ocean.
body: The shield begins with the whole cosmos. The named star-groups, the Pleiades, Hyades, Orion and the Bear, also called the Wain (Wagon), are nearly all that Homer tells us of astronomy; the lines recur almost word for word in Od. 5.272-5, where they guide Odysseus' raft. The Pleiades and Orion were the farmer's and sailor's calendar (Hesiod, Works and Days 383-4, 609-21). Leaf explains why the Bear 'alone' (oiē) has no share in the baths of Ocean, that is, never sets: other circumpolar constellations were inconspicuous and not yet named. Aristotle had already defended the word: 'alone' is a metaphor, 'the best known is called the only one' (Poetics 25, 1461a). The Bear 'watches Orion', the great hunter, as if wary of him. The detail that the Bear never sets was proverbial in later Greek and Latin poetry.

title: The city at peace and the city at war
greek: ἐν δὲ δύω ποίησε πόλεις μερόπων ἀνθρώπων καλάς (en de duō poiēse poleis meropōn anthrōpōn kalas)
short: One city celebrates weddings and settles a homicide by law; the other is besieged and fights over its herds. Together they show the whole of human life.
body: In the first city brides are led by torchlight to the wedding song (humenaios), young men dance and women watch from their doors, and in the assembly a homicide dispute is resolved by public process. In the second, two armies besiege a town; the defenders, with Ares and Athena larger than life at their head (Leaf notes that only these two divinities are named), ambush the herds, and battle follows, with Strife, Tumult and Fate among the fighters. Leaf's Companion notes that, unlike later Greek art, the shield shows scenes of everyday life rather than myth. Ancient readers allegorised the pair: the scholia report that Agallis (or Dalis) of Corcyra took the two cities to be Athens and Eleusis (Eric Cullhed has studied this reading). Taplin argues that the shield sets the war of the Iliad inside a larger world of peace, work and justice that the poem's heroes have lost.

title: The trial scene: a dispute over blood-price (poinē)
greek: δύο δ᾽ ἄνδρες ἐνείκεον εἵνεκα ποινῆς ἀνδρὸς ἀποφθιμένου· ὃ μὲν εὔχετο πάντ᾽ ἀποδοῦναι ... ὃ δ᾽ ἀναίνετο μηδὲν ἑλέσθαι (duo d' andres eneikeon heineka poinēs andros apophthimenou· ho men eucheto pant' apodounai ... ho d' anaineto mēden helesthai)
short: Two men dispute before the people about the price for a killing; the most debated passage in early Greek legal history.
body: Poinē is the compensation a killer paid to the kin of the slain (LSJ); Ajax reminds Akhilleus that a man accepts it even for a brother or son (9.632-6). The Greek of 499-500 is ambiguous. Murray translates 'the one avowed that he had paid all ... the other refused to accept aught', a dispute over a fact. Another reading takes euchomai as 'offered, claimed the right' to pay in full, and the other as refusing to accept any payment, preferring revenge or exile. Leaf's Companion adopts this second view and sees 'criminal law in its very birth': the community asserts its right to decide whether the payment must be accepted. Leaf's note adds that the negative mēden implies an act of will, a refusal, not merely a denial. Later studies (H. J. Wolff, M. Gagarin, R. Westbrook, who compares Near Eastern law) still disagree about what is at issue and who is judging.

anchor: on the word of a daysman
title: The histor ('daysman') and the elders' judgment
greek: ἄμφω δ᾽ ἱέσθην ἐπὶ ἴστορι πεῖραρ ἑλέσθαι (amphō d' hiesthēn epi histori peirar helesthai)
short: Both parties seek a decision 'at the hands of a histor', a 'knower' or arbitrator; the elders give judgment in turn, and two talents await the best.
body: Histōr comes from the root of oida, 'I know', and eidon, 'I saw': one who knows, a witness or arbiter. It is the ancestor of historia, Herodotus' 'inquiry'. Murray's archaic 'daysman' means an umpire, as in the King James Bible: 'Neither is there any daysman betwixt us' (Job 9:33). In 23.486 Idomeneus proposes Agamemnon as histōr of a wager. Leaf's Companion suggests the case was first referred to a single arbiter, perhaps the king, who then called on the council; the elders sit on polished stones 'in the sacred circle', holding heralds' staffs that give the right to speak, and rise to give judgment in turn. Leaf notes that the scene resembles an excited debate more than a modern court. The 'two talents of gold' lie in the middle for the one who speaks 'the straightest judgment' (dikē): Leaf thought them a court fee, too small to be the blood-price itself; this too is disputed.

title: Strife, Tumult and Ker on the battlefield
greek: ἐν δ᾽ Ἔρις ἐν δὲ Κυδοιμὸς ὁμίλεον, ἐν δ᾽ ὀλοὴ Κήρ (en d' Eris en de Kudoimos homileon, en d' oloē Kēr)
short: Personified Strife, Tumult and Ker, the death-spirit, move among the fighters; Ker drags off the wounded and the dead, her cloak red with blood.
body: Murray's 'Fate' translates Kēr, a death-spirit rather than an abstract destiny (moira). She seizes one man fresh-wounded, another unwounded, and drags a corpse by the feet, her garment red 'with the blood of men'. Strife (Eris) and Tumult (Kudoimos) join her; Eris already appeared as a giant figure in 4.440-5 and 11.3-4. Leaf compares the Valkyries of Norse myth and the winged demons who carry off souls on Lycian tombs, and notes that lines 535-8 appear almost word for word in the Hesiodic Shield of Heracles (156-9), so that some critics have thought them copied from there; he holds that the personifications are nonetheless thoroughly epic. The keres of death recur in the Iliad: Akhilleus speaks of his 'two keres' (9.411). On the shield the fighters move 'even as living mortals' and drag away their dead, exactly as the Iliad's warriors do over Patroclus.

title: The golden field that turns black: the marvel of art
greek: ἣ δὲ μελαίνετ᾽ ὄπισθεν, ἀρηρομένῃ δὲ ἐῴκει, χρυσείη περ ἐοῦσα· τὸ δὴ περὶ θαῦμα τέτυκτο (hē de melainet' opisthen, arēromenēi de eōikei, chruseiē per eousa· to dē peri thauma tetukto)
short: Behind the ploughmen the field darkens like freshly turned earth, though it is made of gold: the poet's own comment on art's power to imitate life.
body: Ploughmen drive their teams across a soft fallow field 'thrice ploughed', and at each turn a man hands them a cup of honey-sweet wine. Behind them the earth grows black, 'and seemed verily as it had been ploughed, for all that it was of gold; herein was the great marvel of the work'. This is one of the earliest reflections in Greek literature on mimesis, the power of art to imitate nature: the metal 'becomes' soil. Throughout the shield the scenes do things that no picture can do: they move, speak, sing and change over time; Lessing (Laocoön, ch. 18) admired this as Homer's way of turning description into action. Leaf's Companion reports William Ridgeway's suggestion that the many ploughers show communal ploughing of common land, contrasted with the king's estate in the next scene, and explains the fallow field as part of an alternating two-field system.

title: The king's temenos
greek: ἐν δ᾽ ἐτίθει τέμενος βασιλήϊον (en d' etithei temenos basilēion)
short: A temenos is land 'cut off' for a king or chief; here hired reapers harvest it while the king watches in silence, staff in hand.
body: Temenos, from temnō 'to cut', is 'a piece of land cut off and assigned as an official domain, especially to kings and chiefs' (LSJ, citing this line and the estates granted to Bellerophon, 6.194, and offered to Meleager, 9.578). Later it came to mean land sacred to a god. The word is already Mycenaean: the Linear B tablets from Pylos record a te-me-no, including the wa-na-ka-te-ro te-me-no, the 'temenos of the wanax (king)', on tablet Er 312. Leaf notes a variant reading, 'deep in corn' (bathulēion), and argues that 'royal' gives point to the contrast with the communal ploughing before it; the reapers are erithoi, hired labourers, and Leaf observes that the shield nowhere mentions slaves. The king stands 'in silence, joying in his heart', his staff the sceptre of office, while heralds prepare an ox under an oak for the meal.

title: The Linos-song at the vintage
greek: λίνον δ᾽ ὑπὸ καλὸν ἄειδε λεπταλέῃ φωνῇ (linon d' hupo kalon aeide leptaleēi phōnēi)
short: At the grape-harvest a boy sings the Linos-song, an ancient lament, to the lyre while the young people dance: mourning set within joy.
body: In the vineyard scene a boy plays the lyre and sings 'the beautiful linos'. Aristarchus took linos as a kind of song, like a paean; Zenodotus read linos as the lyre's string (made of flax, linon), 'the string sang sweetly'. Leaf accepts Aristarchus' view, now generally followed. The Linos-song was a lament: Herodotus (2.79) says it was sung in Phoenicia, Cyprus and elsewhere, and that the Egyptians called it Maneros, a dirge for a king's son who died young; a Hesiodic fragment quoted in the scholia says all singers and lyre-players lament Linus at feasts and dances. Leaf connects it with laments for the departing summer, like the Near Eastern wailing for Tammuz. A dirge at a harvest festival is a characteristic Iliadic touch.

title: The dancing-floor of Daedalus and Ariadne
greek: τῷ ἴκελον οἷόν ποτ᾽ ἐνὶ Κνωσῷ εὐρείῃ Δαίδαλος ἤσκησεν καλλιπλοκάμῳ Ἀριάδνῃ ... παρθένοι ἀλφεσίβοιαι (tōi ikelon hoion pot' eni Knōsōi eureiēi Daidalos ēskēsen kalliplokamōi Ariadnēi ... parthenoi alphesiboiai)
short: Hephaestus makes a dance like the one Daedalus once made at Knossos for Ariadne; young men and 'cattle-earning' maidens circle like a potter's wheel.
body: This is the only scene on the shield linked to a named place and myth. Choros can mean both the dance and the dancing-floor. Daedalus, the legendary craftsman of Minoan Crete, made it for Ariadne, daughter of Minos; Pausanias (9.40.3) saw at Knossos a relief in white marble of 'Ariadne's Dance' attributed to Daedalus. Leaf stresses that Crete was famed for dancing and that the scholia call the tumblers and armed dance Cretan; some critics therefore thought 590-605 a Cretan interpolation. The maidens are alphesiboiai, 'earning oxen' for their parents as bride-price (hedna) (LSJ; Leaf). The dancers run in a circle as smoothly as a potter tries his wheel, then in lines toward each other; some have connected the figures with the 'crane dance' Theseus led on Delos in imitation of the Labyrinth.

title: The two tumblers and the missing singer
greek: δοιὼ δὲ κυβιστητῆρε κατ᾽ αὐτοὺς μολπῆς ἐξάρχοντες ἐδίνευον κατὰ μέσσους (doiō de kubistētēre kat' autous molpēs exarchontes edineuon kata messous)
short: Two acrobats lead the dance. Many editions add 'a divine singer' here on Athenaeus' authority, but Murray, following the manuscripts, does not.
body: Kubistētēr means 'tumbler' (LSJ; the same word is used mockingly of a man falling headlong like a diver, 16.750). The two tumblers 'lead off the song-and-dance' (molpēs exarchontes) and whirl through the middle. Since F. A. Wolf, editors have inserted before this a line from Od. 4.17-18, 'and among them a divine minstrel sang to the lyre', because Athenaeus (5.181c) claimed that Aristarchus had cut the singer out of this 'Cretan dance'. Leaf rejects the insertion: the line is in no manuscript, and the genuine text makes the tumblers the leaders. Murray's translation follows the manuscripts. Leaf's Companion compares the Easter dances at Megara, where each line of dancers is led by one virtuoso. Martin Revermann has re-examined the question, arguing that debate has focused too narrowly on Athenaeus. Whether a bard stands on the shield matters for how the poem pictures its own art.

title: Greaves of pliant tin; the arms delivered
greek: τεῦξε δέ οἱ κνημῖδας ἑανοῦ κασσιτέροιο (teuxe de hoi knēmidas heanou kassiteroio)
short: Hephaestus completes a fiery corselet, a gold-crested helmet and greaves of soft tin; Thetis swoops from Olympus like a falcon with the gleaming arms.
body: After the shield come a corselet 'brighter than the blaze of fire', a heavy helmet with a golden crest and greaves of 'pliant' (heanos) tin. Tin is a soft metal, and the epithet heanos is elsewhere used of fine robes, which puzzled critics. Leaf reports W. Reichel's explanation that Homeric knēmides were not armour against missiles but gaiters protecting the shins from the edge of the great body-shield, so softness was no defect. Aristotle discusses a related phrase, 'greaves of new-wrought tin' (21.592), among problems solved by recognising loose usage (Poetics 25, 1461a). Book 18 ends with a swift descent: Thetis springs from snowy Olympus 'like a falcon', bearing the flashing armour. The arms that begin Book 19 are the gift that makes Akhilleus' return to battle, and his death, possible.
